sections.title: The verb agrees with its subject

body.p: The verb ending matches the **person** and **number** of the subject.

ex.el: Ο Νίκος δουλεύει. — Ο Νίκος και η Ελένη δουλεύουν.
ex.en: Nikos works. — Nikos and Eleni work.

ex.el: Εσύ κι εγώ θα πάμε μαζί.
ex.en: You and I will go together.

list: Two subjects joined by **και** take a plural verb. If one of them is **εγώ**, the verb is 1st person plural (**εσύ κι εγώ ... πάμε**); if one is **εσύ** (and no εγώ), 2nd person plural (**εσύ κι ο Νίκος ... πάτε**).
**Neuter plurals** take a plural verb in Modern Greek: **Τα σπίτια είναι παλιά.** (Ancient Greek used the singular; you will meet this only in quotations.)
With **με** "with", speech often uses the plural too: **Ο Νίκος με τη Μαρία ήρθαν μαζί.** Writing prefers **Ο Νίκος ήρθε με τη Μαρία.**

check.q: "My brother and I live in Athens."
options: Ο αδερφός μου κι εγώ μένουν στην Αθήνα.
Ο αδερφός μου κι εγώ μένουμε στην Αθήνα.
Ο αδερφός μου κι εγώ μένω στην Αθήνα.
check.answer: Ο αδερφός μου κι εγώ μένουμε στην Αθήνα.
check.why: With εγώ among the subjects, the verb is "we": μένουμε.
Neuter plural subject, plural verb, neuter plural adjective.

check.answer: Εσύ κι ο Νίκος θα έρθετε.
accept: Εσύ και ο Νίκος θα έρθετε.
check.why: εσύ + someone else = εσείς: θα έρθετε.

sections.title: The predicate after είμαι: the nominative

body.p: After **είμαι, γίνομαι** "become", **φαίνομαι** "seem", **λέγομαι** "be called", **μένω** "remain" the predicate is in the **nominative** and agrees with the subject.
No article and no **ένας** with professions and roles after είμαι: **Είναι δασκάλα** "She is a teacher".
**Polite εσείς** takes a plural verb but the adjective agrees with the real person: **Είστε κουρασμένος, κύριε;** "Are you tired, sir?" **Είστε έτοιμη, κυρία Παπαδάκη;**

check.why: A profession after είναι: nominative, no article.

check.q: To a woman, politely: "Are you ready?"
check.why: Plural verb, but the adjective agrees with the one woman: έτοιμη.
Nominative neuter plural predicate.

head: Case
Role
Example
rows: direct object; after almost every preposition; time and measure
Βλέπω **τον φίλο μου**. Πάω **στον φίλο μου**. Έμεινα **δύο μέρες**.
possessor; indirect object (person who receives); after some formal prepositions
Το σπίτι **του φίλου μου**. **Του** έδωσα το κλειδί.

body.p: The **accusative without a preposition** also expresses **time** and **measure**:

ex.en: On Monday I go to work.
I work eight hours a day.

body.p: A container and its content stand side by side in the same case, with no "of": **ένα ποτήρι νερό** "a glass of water", **δύο κιλά ντομάτες**, **ένα μπουκάλι κρασί**.

check.q: "On Sunday we're going to the beach."
check.why: Days as time expressions: accusative, no preposition.

options: ένα φλιτζάνι του καφέ (= a cup for coffee)
check.why: Container + content: same case, no preposition. (φλιτζάνι του καφέ means "a coffee cup".)
Duration: plain accusative.

sections.el: Το έμμεσο αντικείμενο: σε ή γενική
sections.title: The indirect object: σε + accusative or the genitive

body.p: The person who receives or is addressed ("to whom") is expressed in two ways:

head: Form
Example
Use
rows: colloquial, northern Greek; avoid in writing

body.p: Verbs that take this "to whom": **δίνω, λέω, στέλνω, γράφω, δείχνω, εξηγώ, τηλεφωνώ, απαντώ, μιλάω, χρωστάω, υπόσχομαι, δανείζω**.

ex.en: I spoke to the director. — I spoke to him.
I owe the bank. — I owe it.

check.why: τηλεφωνώ takes σε + accusative (or a genitive pronoun).
The person shown to: genitive weak pronoun μας after the imperative. (Δείξε τις φωτογραφίες μας = "show our photos".)

check.q: Replace the noun with a pronoun: Έστειλα ένα μήνυμα στον Πέτρο.
check.why: σε + noun becomes a genitive weak pronoun before the verb.

body.p: Some very common verbs put the **person who feels** in the genitive (or σε + accusative) and the **thing** in the nominative, as the subject. The verb then agrees with the thing.

head: Verb
Example
Literally
rows: Μου αρέσουν τα σύκα. "I like figs."
Μου φαίνεται δύσκολο. "It seems hard to me."
Με πονάει το κεφάλι μου. / Πονάει το κεφάλι μου. "I have a headache."
Το σπίτι ανήκει στον παππού. "The house belongs to grandpa."
Μου χρειάζονται λεφτά. / Χρειάζομαι λεφτά. "I need money."
Δεν μου κάνει το παντελόνι. "The trousers don't fit me."

ex.en: Did you like the films? (plural verb: the films)

body.tip: "I miss you" is **Μου λείπεις**: **you** are the subject (λείπεις), **I** am the genitive (μου). English learners often say ***Σου λείπω**, which means "You miss me".

check.why: The shoes are the subject, so the verb is plural: αρέσουν.
The parents are the subject (λείπουν); she is the genitive της.
You (plural) are the subject: λείπετε; I am μου.

sections.el: Δύο αιτιατικές και κατηγορούμενο του αντικειμένου
sections.title: Two accusatives and the object predicate

body.p: A few verbs take **two accusatives**: the person and the thing.
Verbs of **naming, choosing, considering, making** take an object and a **predicate in the accusative** (the object's description):
In the **passive** both turn into nominatives: **Θεωρείται έξυπνος** "He is considered clever", **Εξελέγη δήμαρχος** "He was elected mayor".

links.el: Ρήματα με δύο αντικείμενα και κατηγορούμενο
links.title: Double objects and object complements

check.why: Object and its predicate both in the accusative.
In the passive the predicate is nominative.
The object predicate agrees in the accusative (neuter άδειο).

sections.el: Η γενική ως ρόλος στην πρόταση
sections.title: The genitive in sentence roles

body.p: Besides possession and the indirect object, the genitive does a lot of work in formal Greek:

list: **Subject or object of a noun**: **η άφιξη του πλοίου** "the arrival of the ship" (the ship arrives), **η κατασκευή της γέφυρας** "the building of the bridge" (someone builds the bridge). This is the heart of the nominal style.

**After formal prepositions and adverbs**: **κατά τη διάρκεια της συνάντησης**, **εξαιτίας του καιρού**, **λόγω της απεργίας**, **εναντίον του νόμου**, **μεταξύ των δύο χωρών**, **εντός της προθεσμίας**, **υπέρ της πρότασης**.
**Time**: **του χρόνου** "next year", **της Παναγίας** "on the Feast of the Assumption".
**Quality and material in set phrases**: **άνθρωπος της εμπιστοσύνης μου** "someone I trust", **κοστούμι του γάμου**.

ex.el: Λόγω της απεργίας, τα πλοία μένουν δεμένα.
ex.en: Because of the strike, the ships are staying in port.

ex.el: Η αύξηση των τιμών ανησυχεί τους καταναλωτές.
ex.en: The rise in prices worries consumers.
She is two years older than me.

sections.title: Learned case uses and frozen datives

body.p: The dative has gone from the living language, but many fixed phrases keep it. You must recognise them and use them as wholes; they do not combine with modern case rules.

list: **Genitive absolute-like phrases** with participles: **δοθείσης της ευκαιρίας** "since the opportunity has arisen", **λαμβανομένου υπόψη ότι** "taking into account that". They belong to formal writing and speeches.
**Accusative of respect**: **Είναι Έλληνας την καταγωγή** "He is Greek by origin", **γιατρός το επάγγελμα** "a doctor by profession", **ψηλός το ανάστημα**.

ex.el: Η απόφαση πάρθηκε εν αγνοία μου.
ex.en: The decision was taken without my knowledge.

title: Agreement and case in the sentence
blurb: Who agrees with whom, the four cases as sentence roles, verbs that take the genitive or two accusatives, predicates after είμαι and θεωρώ, and the frozen datives of formal Greek.

intro.p: Declension tables tell you the forms; this guide tells you **which form the sentence needs**. Greek grammar ties the verb to its subject (person and number), the adjective to its noun (gender, number, case), and each noun phrase to its role (nominative subject, accusative object, genitive possessor or recipient). Once you see the roles, choosing the case becomes a matter of asking one question: what is this phrase doing in the sentence?
